line: Bridges. Thirty years, mostly the river crossings for the state. Everyone looks at the deck. I looked at what holds it up.
choice1: Did you come here for the work?

line: In 1994, for a job that was supposed to last two years. Then another job. Then my daughter was in school, and that was that. We've come to this park since the first summer.

line: The tables are new. The people are the same kind, old men who think they're winning. Walt sat down at my table three summers ago and asked what the river was for. We've argued ever since.

line: Everyone here says it's impossible. Old Wu says the paper printed it wrong. Do you play?

line: Chariot to the river. You give it away. $ [neutral] No? Nobody sees it. My father liked problems like this. He'd leave one on the kitchen table before work.
choice1: What did you do for work?

line: He came alone, after his wife died. His sons are in California. Thursdays he has me and the board. If he wants to move a horse twice, fine.
You again. Old Wu is late and his tea is getting cold, so I'm drinking it. Don't tell him.
At the doctor. Blood pressure. Dr. Zhou took it at the Saturday talk and sent him straight there.
choice2: I hope he's okay. See you.

line: He says yes. He also says the paper printed the problem wrong. I trust him on neither.
choice1: Do you come here every day?

line: Mornings the park, afternoons here, when my wife allows. In the park I play Walt's chess. Here I get the real one, and somebody to complain to in Chinese.
I'd be bored with only one. Here everybody knows my wife's cooking and my father's village. In the park nobody knows anything, and Walt asks about the river every year like it's new.
You again. Sit. The problem in the paper is easy today. Even Old Wu got it.
Putting his name down. Mr. Guo is making the festival list, and if you're not on the list, on Thursday he looks at you like you owe him money.

She caught me in May. _sets up the pieces_ She plays like a chariot: straight down the board, across the river, to the library, city hall, anywhere. Good. Somebody should. $ [neutral] But a chariot alone gets taken. Guo still minds the palace while she's out.

You again. Good. Walt only plays one opening. It's very boring to beat him.
The Ruy Lopez. Every time, three years now. I tell him, try something. He says why, it works. _shrugs_ It does work. That's the annoying part.

line: Sit. Five minutes, until he comes. You take white.
Hm. You hold your pieces back, like my daughter. She only plays on the phone now, against strangers in other countries.
She learned it from me, at six. Now chess, on the phone. Her boy is two, so nothing yet. My wife says don't push. I'm not pushing. I bought a small board, that's all.

line: Ah, {playerName}. Sit. I want to show you something.
This. _unfolds a square of cardboard from his jacket_ My father's board. The lines are drawn with a ruler and a pen. I bring it when I play with someone I like.

line: My wife wants to throw it out every spring, so it lives in my jacket. Thirty years here and it's the only thing I brought that I still use.
choice1: Do you miss where you grew up?
choice2: Keep it in the jacket. See you.

line: Not the way people think. My daughter is here, the boy, this park. $ [guarded] But my father wrote the date on the side, 1961, in his hand. If I lost this I don't know what I would do.

line: Next time. Bring tea. Walt can wait for once.
Hello. Sit if you want. But quietly today.
Hello. Excuse the noise. I'm speaking loudly today, on purpose.
My wife says don't speak Chinese loudly in the park now, since the speeches. I said we've been in this park since 1994. She says speak quietly anyway.

line: Last week I called across the path to Old Wu, and two young men at the next table said something. Not to me. About me.
Nothing. I moved my horse. Walt heard it. He told them the table was reserved. It isn't reserved. _a small smile_ He's a very bad liar, so they believed him.
Good afternoon. Did you hear the radio this morning?

line: The new president will clear the citizenship backlog, they say. Twelve months, they say.

choice2: We'll see. See you, Mr. Lin.

line: My sister. Eleven years she has waited. She calls on the first of the month to ask if I heard anything. I hear what the radio hears.

line: She wants to vote once before she's seventy. She's sixty-eight. I'll believe the radio when she calls me with the letter in her hand.
